sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We use the following notations:

  • [MATH: y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x] is the regression line that best fits the population, and

  • [MATH: \widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x] is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that

[MATH: \widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x.]

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the slope [MATH: \beta_1] of our model can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] }^{\textrm{margin of error}}.]

Note the following:

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,\beta}_1] is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

  • [MATH: P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] where [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-2] degrees of freedom.

  • [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]] is the standard error of [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1,] given by [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{ \dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}] where we have:

    • [MATH: \textrm{MSE}] is the mean squared error of the model: [MATH: \textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2] where [MATH: \widehat{\,y}_i] is the estimate of [MATH: y_i] given by our regression model.

    • [MATH: S_{xx}] is the usual sum of squares formula: [MATH: \displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2]

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

  • Step 1. Find the point estimate. From the regression equation [MATH: \widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7 x,] our point estimate is
    [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 = 0.7.]

  • Step 2. Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval, we have [MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.] We are given that [MATH: P(T > 1.943) = 0.05.] As a result, [MATH: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943.] Now, we can compute the margin of error: [MATH: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 1.943 \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{1.25}{42}} \approx 0.3]

  • Step 3. Determine the limits of the confidence interval: [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = 0.7 \pm 0.3]

[MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] }^{\textrm{margin of error}}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we conduct a random sample of [MATH: n] of paired observations [MATH: (x_i,y_i)] drawn from a population.

Content:
[MATH: (x_1,y_1), \quad (x_2,y_2), \quad \ldots, \quad (x_n,y_n)]

Content:
Using previously discussed techniques, we can calculate the linear regression line for this data, which we'll denote as

Content:
[MATH: y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x.]

Content:
Our estimates for the slope parameter [MATH: \widehat{\beta_1}] and intercept parameter [MATH: \widehat{\beta_0}] are given by

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\beta_1} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta_0} = \overline{y} - \widehat{\beta_1}\overline{x},]

Content:
where [MATH: \overline{x}] and [MATH: \overline{y}] are the mean values of [MATH: x_i] and [MATH: y_i,] and the quantities [MATH: S_{xx}] and [MATH: S_{xy}] are given by
[MATH: S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2,
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}).]

Content:
Plotting our regression line alongside the sample data, we might get a diagram similar to the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/de526db6d561c19243d7f2fffeee266a]

Content:
Notice that we referred to [MATH: \widehat{\beta_0}] and [MATH: \widehat{\beta_1}] as estimates. This is because if we were to conduct a census on the population, we'd be able to calculate the "true" regression equation for the data that considers every population member. We'll denote this "true" regression line as

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.]

Content:
The two lines are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/598bbdb348943456314e402c8091c960]

Content:
To summarize,

Content:
- the regression equation [MATH: y = \widehat{\beta_0} + \widehat{\beta_1} x] is an estimate of the true regression equation [MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x,]
- [MATH: \widehat{\beta_1}] is an estimate of the "true" slope parameter [MATH: \beta_1,] and
- [MATH: \widehat{\beta_0}] is an estimate of the "true" intercept parameter [MATH: \beta_0.]

Content:
In this lesson, we will learn how to construct confidence intervals for the slope parameter [MATH: \beta_1.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Summary of the Key Result

Content:
Given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the slope [MATH: \beta_1] of our model can be written as

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] }^{\textrm{margin of error}}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,\beta}_1] is our point estimate for the slope, computed by fitting the data points from our sample.
- [MATH: P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] where [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-2] degrees of freedom.
- [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]] is the standard error of [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1,] given by
[MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{ \dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}]
where we have:

- [MATH: \textrm{MSE}] is the so-called mean squared error of the model, given by
[MATH: \textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2,]
where [MATH: \widehat{\,y}_i] is the estimate of [MATH: y_i] given by our regression model.
- [MATH: S_{xx}] is the usual sum of squares formula:
[MATH: \displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2]

Content:
The derivation of this result is rather long, and we leave it until the end of the lesson. For now, note the following:

Content:
- Each data point in the sample has some residual (i.e., error) associated with it. The error of our regression model at the data point [MATH: (x_i,y_i)] is given by
[MATH: (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i).]
- The expression [MATH: \displaystyle\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2] gives the sum of the squared residuals of our regression model.
- Even considering the entire population, the data points will not fall on a perfectly straight line. Thus, errors are present even in the "true" regression model. These errors have some (unknown) variance, which we'll denote as [MATH: \sigma^2.]
- It can be shown that the [MATH: \textrm{MSE}] is an unbiased estimator of [MATH: \sigma^2.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Finding Confidence Intervals for Slope Parameters

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: \widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x] be the regression line fitted using a sample [MATH: (x_1,y_1), \: \ldots, \: (x_{8},y_{8})] of [MATH: n=8] paired observations. Assuming that all conditions for the simple regression model are satisfied, the mean square error of the model is [MATH: 1.25,] and [MATH: S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2 = 42,] find a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval for the slope of the regression line.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(T > 1.943) = 0.05,] where [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: 6] degrees of freedom. Also, the standard error for [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1] is given by [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{ \dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the following notations:

- [MATH: y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 x] is the regression line that best fits the population, and
- [MATH: \widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x] is the estimate of the "true" regression line given by the data in our sample.

In this case, we have that

[MATH: \widehat{\,y}=\widehat{\,\beta}_0+\widehat{\,\beta}_1x=1.6+0.7 x.]

We are told that all assumptions for a simple regression model are held. So, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the slope [MATH: \beta_1] of our model can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 \: \pm \: \overbrace{t_{n-2,\alpha/2} \cdot \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] }^{\textrm{margin of error}}.]

Note the following:

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,\beta}_1] is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.
- [MATH: P(T > t_{n-2,\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2},] where [MATH: T] has a student's [MATH: t]-distribution with [MATH: n-2] degrees of freedom.
- [MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,]] is the standard error of [MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1,] given by
[MATH: \textrm{SE}[\widehat{\,\beta}_1\,] = \sqrt{ \dfrac{\textrm{MSE}}{S_{xx}}}]
where we have:

- [MATH: \textrm{MSE}] is the mean squared error of the model:
[MATH: \textrm{MSE} = \dfrac{1}{n-2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\,y}_i)^2]
where [MATH: \widehat{\,y}_i] is the estimate of [MATH: y_i] given by our regression model.
- [MATH: S_{xx}] is the usual sum of squares formula:
[MATH: \displaystyle S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})^2]

To construct the confidence interval, we proceed as follows:

- Step 1. Find the point estimate. From the regression equation [MATH: \widehat{\,y}=1.6+0.7 x,] our point estimate is
[MATH: \widehat{\,\beta}_1 = 0.7.]
- Step 2. Find the margin of error. Since we are interested in finding a [MATH: 90\%] confidence interval, we have
[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]
We are given that [MATH: P(T > 1.943) = 0.05.] As a result,
[MATH: t_{n-2,\alpha/2} = t_{6,0.05} = 1.943.]
Now, we can compute the margin of error:

Note the following:

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,\beta}_1] is our point estimate for the slope, computed using the data points from our sample.

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.05.]

Content:
[MATH: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.]

For each [MATH: i=1,2,\ldots,n,] let

Content:

Content:
Earlier, we made use of the following results:

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E[\widehat{\beta}_1] = \beta_1,
\qquad
\textrm{Var}[\widehat{\beta_1}] = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}]

Content:
Let's now derive these. First, we will show that

Content:
[MATH: S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})y_i.]

Content:
We can show this is true using some straightforward manipulations of the summation, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: S_{xy}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))(y_{i} − y^(―)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i} − ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y^(―); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i} − y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―)); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i} − y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i} − y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)nx^(―); = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i} − y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + y^(―)∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} − x^(―))y_{i}.]

Content:
Using our result for [MATH: S_{xy},] we can write

Content:
[MATH: β_{1}^(^) = (S_{xy})/(S_{xx}) = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}]
where

Content:
[MATH: k_i = \dfrac{ x_i-\overline{x}}{S_{xx}}.]

Content:
The following properties can be shown using straightforward algebra:

Content:
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i=0]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i x_i=1]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^n k_i^2=\dfrac{1}{S_{xx}}]

Content:
Now, we compute the mean and variance of [MATH: \widehat{\beta_1}] as follows:

Content:
- For the mean, we have
[MATH: E[β_{1}^(^)]|= E[∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}]; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}E[y_{i}]; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}(β_{0} + β_{1}x_{i}); = β_{0}∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i} + β_{1}∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{1}x_{i}; = β_{0} ⋅ 0 + β_{1} ⋅ 1; = β_{1}.]
Note that we used the properties of [MATH: k_i] discussed previously.
- For the variance, we have
[MATH: Var[β_{1}^(^)]|= Var[∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}y_{i}]; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}^{2}Var[y_{i}]; = ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}^{2} ⋅ σ^{2}; = σ^{2} ⋅ ∑_(i = 1)^(n)k_{i}^{2}; = (σ^{2})/(S_{xx}).]

Content:
So, finally, we have

Content:
[MATH: \widehat{\beta_1} \sim N\left(\beta_1, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}\right).]
